title: Malpractice Insurance
path: Health Care Financing and Insurance Scheme

headings.title: Introduction to Malpractice Insurance in Nursing
headings.content: Malpractice insurance, often called professional liability insurance, is a specific type of coverage designed to protect nurses from financial loss if they are sued for professional negligence. In Nigerian healthcare settings, nurses face increasing legal scrutiny from patients and families who are more aware of their rights. While the **Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN)** regulates practice standards, professional liability coverage steps in when civil claims arise. Many practitioners wrongly assume that hospital indemnity is enough. Employer policies typically protect the institution first, leaving the individual nurse exposed if a lawsuit names them personally. Securing independent protection ensures dedicated legal representation and covers court settlements or damages.

headings.title: Key Legal and Ethical Concepts in Nursing Practice
headings.content: Understanding professional liability requires a firm grasp of foundational legal duties. **Negligence** occurs when a nurse fails to act as a reasonably prudent nurse would under similar circumstances. **Malpractice** is a specialized form of negligence applied to licensed professionals. To successfully claim malpractice in court, a plaintiff must prove four elements: duty, breach of duty, causation, and injury. Ethical principles like **beneficence** (doing good) and **non-maleficence** (doing no harm) guide daily bedside decisions. Failing to uphold these duties breaches the standard of care and exposes the clinician to severe legal penalties.

headings.title: Types of Malpractice Insurance Policies: Claims-Made versus Occurrence
headings.content:
- **Occurrence Policies**: Cover incidents that happened during the period the policy was active, even if the lawsuit is filed years later after the policy has expired or been cancelled.
- **Claims-Made Policies**: Cover incidents only if both the event and the resulting lawsuit happen while the policy is active. If you cancel a claims-made policy, you lose coverage unless you purchase supplemental 'tail' insurance.

Selecting the right policy structure prevents dangerous gaps in coverage upon retirement or job transition.

headings.title: Common Liability Risks and Claims in Nursing
headings.content: Clinical errors happen in high-stress environments, but certain mistakes frequently trigger lawsuits. Medication administration errors remain a leading cause of liability, whether involving incorrect dosages, wrong routes, or omitted drugs. Failing to monitor patients adequately after high-risk procedures or ignoring sudden changes in vital signs also invites legal action. Documentation mistakes are equally dangerous; unrecorded care is legally interpreted as care that was never performed. Patient falls resulting in severe trauma often lead to litigation if safety protocols like bed rails or call bells were ignored.

headings.title: Employer-Provided Coverage versus Individual Policies
headings.content:
| Feature | Employer-Provided Policy | Individual Policy |
|---|---|---|>
| **Primary Loyalty** | Protects the healthcare institution | Protects the individual nurse exclusively |
| **Cost** | Usually free or heavily subsidized | Paid entirely by the nurse |
| **Portability** | Lost immediately upon leaving the job | Stays with the nurse across job changes |
| **Limits** | Shared pool of coverage for all staff | Dedicated limits solely for the policyholder |

Relying on institutional coverage leaves gaps if multiple staff members are named in a single severe lawsuit, draining the shared policy limit.

headings.title: Risk Management Strategies to Prevent Malpractice Claims
headings.content:
- **Maintain Clear Communication**: Practice open, honest dialogue with patients and multidisciplinary team members.
- **Adhere to Standards**: Follow evidence-based hospital protocols and clinical guidelines strictly.
- **Document Accurately**: Record objective findings, patient responses, and exact times of interventions promptly.
- **Verify Orders**: Clarify ambiguous or unsafe medication orders with the prescribing physician before administration.
- **Know Your Scope**: Never perform clinical tasks outside your legal scope of practice or without proper training.

Proactive risk reduction protects patients from harm and shields nurses from litigation.
